briefing.text: Lesion type is not a clinical column: CANCER_TYPE_DETAILED reads 'Invasive Breast Carcinoma' for every sample, including JP and DCIS. Take lesion type from the SAMPLE_ID suffix (-JP, -DCIS, -IDC). Only patient JuP3 has a matched JP, DCIS and IDC. JuP1 and JuP2 have one unsuffixed sample each. The hypothesis is about JP versus its associated DCIS and IDC, so the main comparison is within JuP3 (JuP3-JP vs JuP3-DCIS vs JuP3-IDC). Do not pool the unmatched samples into a JP group, and state that one matched trio supports only a descriptive comparison.
briefing.reason: Grouping by the clinical column or pooling unmatched samples would give the wrong comparison.

briefing.text: data_cna_hg19.seg contains segmented copy number for JuP3-JP, JuP3-DCIS and JuP3-IDC (and for JuP1 and JuP2), so CNA burden per lesion can be computed. The relevant variable therefore exists. If JP shows fewer or similar CNAs than its matched DCIS/IDC, that counts as evidence against the hypothesis, not as grounds for 'Not verifiable'.
briefing.reason: This prevents a wrong 'Not verifiable' label and clarifies what counts as contrary evidence.

briefing.text: Counting raw .seg rows measures segmentation, not alterations, and many segments may be copy-neutral. For each sample, compute (a) the number of segments, (b) the number of segments with |seg.mean| above a threshold, and (c) the fraction of genome altered (bp with |seg.mean| > threshold divided by total bp). Also tabulate num.mark and segment length, and recount after excluding small or low-marker segments (e.g. num.mark<10 or <1 Mb). Base the conclusion on called alterations, and report it as metric-dependent if the metrics disagree on direction.
briefing.reason: The choice of CNA burden metric and noise filtering can decide the direction of the comparison.

briefing.text: CNA calls from log2 seg.mean depend on the threshold (cBioPortal FGA uses 0.1, CNVkit uses gain>0.2 and loss<-0.25, others use ±0.3). Recompute thresholded counts and FGA at 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3, plus high-level cutoffs, for the three JuP3 lesions. Check whether the JP vs DCIS/IDC ordering holds across thresholds, and say so explicitly if it flips.
briefing.reason: The ranking may change with the cutoff, which affects how confident a True/False call can be.

briefing.text: Check each sample's length-weighted median seg.mean. It should be near 0. If it is not, recentre by subtracting it before thresholding, and report whether the conclusions change.
briefing.reason: A shifted baseline can create or erase apparent genome-wide alterations in one lesion.

briefing.text: No tumour purity values are provided. Normal-cell contamination pulls log2 ratios toward 0, so a lower-cellularity lesion can show fewer events above a fixed threshold. Compare the per-sample |seg.mean| distribution (max, 95th percentile) and check whether the same loci are altered at different amplitudes across the lesions. Note this limitation in the reasoning, but still report the observed burden.
briefing.reason: Without this check, amplitude differences could be misread as differences in the number of alterations.

shared_assumptions: Both teams assumed |seg.mean| thresholds on log2 ratios measure CNA burden the same way in all three JuP3 lesions. Low tumour cellularity in JuP3-JP would scale its log2 ratios towards 0, and neither team tested or corrected for that.

Both teams assumed the comparison set is the JuP3 trio, which matches the wording 'associated'. JuP1 and JuP2 (unsuffixed, labelled the same as all samples) were treated as JP context by team B without checking from the data that they are JP lesions.
Both teams assumed 'number of copy number alterations' means genome-wide burden (FGA or thresholded segments), not a count of discrete events such as breakpoints or arm-level and focal events.
unused_evidence: TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS in data_clinical_sample.txt: JuP3-JP has a much lower value than DCIS and IDC. A uniformly low signal in both mutations and CNAs fits low JP purity as well as a truly quiet genome, and neither team used it to tell these apart.

data_mutations.txt: JuP3-JP has only 3 calls. Neither team checked whether these are shared with DCIS/IDC (clonal relatedness) or noted that t_ref_count/t_alt_count are empty for every row, which rules out purity estimation from VAF.
num.mark and breakpoint positions: team A filtered on them, but neither team compared breakpoint locations of JP with DCIS/IDC as a purity-independent count.
unresolved_weak_points: Team A named low JP purity as its weakest point and argued against it from the absence of DCIS/IDC arm events in JP. A JP lesion that is clonally separate from DCIS/IDC would also lack shared events, so this does not rule out low purity.
Team B named low purity as its weakest point and only reported it. It ran no check.
second_readings: 'High number of CNAs' could mean a count of discrete segments or breakpoints rather than fraction of genome altered. Team A reports that at |0.1| the JP segment count (18) roughly equals DCIS (18) and IDC (17), so the count reading and the FGA reading may not agree.

'Compared to associated DCIS and IDC-NST' could be read as an absolute claim ('high', e.g. relative to typical breast lesions) or as a strict ranking above both. The label depends on which reading is used.
challenge.verdict: Moderate trust. Both teams use FGA within the one matched trio, and the direction holds across thresholds. However, n=1, JP's uniformly low signal (low TMB, only 3 mutations, max |seg.mean| 0.21) fits low purity as well as a quiet genome, read counts are empty, and the raw segment-count reading puts JP level with DCIS/IDC.

questions.question: QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Your raw segment count at |0.1| puts JP level with DCIS and IDC (18/18/17). Count breakpoints per lesion after merging adjacent segments whose seg.mean differs by less than a fixed noise margin, restricted to segments with num.mark>=10. Does the JP ranking on this breakpoint count agree with the FGA ranking, and if not, does that change which metric your label rests on?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Do JuP3-JP's 3 mutations also appear in JuP3-DCIS or JuP3-IDC (same chromosome, position and allele)? If none are shared, your argument that missing shared arm events in JP rules out low purity no longer holds. Does that change how you handle the purity weak point?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS is far lower in JuP3-JP than in DCIS/IDC, and t_ref_count/t_alt_count are empty. Count non-empty read-count values to confirm this. Given that no purity estimate exists, does the joint low TMB and low CNA amplitude make you reword or relabel the conclusion?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Scale JP's seg.mean values by a range of assumed purity factors, for example asking what factor would bring JP's maximum |seg.mean| to DCIS's level. Then recompute FGA at your thresholds. At what assumed purity does the ranking flip, and is that purity plausible enough to change your label or confidence?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: You used JuP1/JuP2 as JP context. What in the data, as opposed to an assumption, shows they are JP lesions? If nothing does, does dropping them change your method or confidence?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Tabulate the per-lesion count of segments and breakpoints (not FGA) at your thresholds, after excluding segments with few markers. Does JP's rank on counts agree with its rank on FGA? The hypothesis speaks of a 'number' of alterations: if the two disagree, which one does your label rest on?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: You listed low JP purity as your weakest point but ran no check. Check whether JuP3-JP's mutations are shared with DCIS/IDC, and compare TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS across the trio. Do these results make low purity more or less likely, and do they change your label or confidence?

QUESTION FROM THE DIRECTOR: Recompute FGA after scaling JP's seg.mean by a range of assumed purity factors. At what factor does JP's FGA match DCIS or IDC, and does that sensitivity change your conclusion?

In copy-number analysis of tumour sequencing data, how does tumour cellularity (purity) attenuate segment log2 ratios, and what methods estimate purity from exome data when allele read counts are unavailable?
questions.why: Both teams' conclusion rests on low log2 amplitudes in one lesion. Whether low purity alone could explain this, and whether it can be checked without VAFs, is unresolved.

questions.question: In cancer-genomics papers, when a lesion is said to show a 'high number of copy number alterations', is that usually measured as the count of CNA segments or events, or as fraction of genome altered?
questions.why: The two metrics may rank the lesions differently here, so the metric convention decides which reading of the hypothesis is tested.

findings.question: In copy-number analysis of tumour sequencing data, how does tumour cellularity (purity) attenuate segment log2 ratios, and what methods estimate purity from exome data when allele read counts are unavailable?
findings.answer: Normal-cell contamination pulls observed copy ratios toward 1 (log2 toward 0). For a diploid genome, observed ratio = (p*CN_tumour + (1-p)*2)/2. A single-copy loss is log2(1/2) = -1.0 when pure but log2(0.75) = -0.415 at 50% purity; a single-copy gain is +0.585 when pure and smaller as purity falls. So low purity alone can explain low log2 amplitudes, and amplitude alone cannot tell low purity apart from subclonality or genuinely few or small CNAs. Without VAFs or BAFs, purity can be estimated from read depth only: (a) the log2 values of clonal CNAs cluster at levels set by purity and ploidy (CNVkit docs approach 4; ABSOLUTE fits purity and ploidy from segmented copy number plus karyotype priors); (b) AITAC estimates purity from read depths in deleted regions alone; (c) a pathologist's cellularity estimate. Fits from copy number alone are ambiguous between purity and ploidy and less reliable than allele-based methods. Sequenza, PurityEst, PurBayes, TPES and THetA2 (BAF mode) need allele or SNV data. A rough check with no allele data: if a lesion's strongest clonal-looking losses sit near -0.4 rather than -1, that fits about 50% purity.

SOURCES: https://cnvkit.readthedocs.io/en/stable/heterogeneity.html, https://cnvkit.readthedocs.io/en/stable/calling.html, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7205152/.

findings.question: In cancer-genomics papers, when a lesion is said to show a 'high number of copy number alterations', is that usually measured as the count of CNA segments or events, or as fraction of genome altered?
findings.answer: The web does not settle a single convention. Both are in common use: event or segment counts (e.g. CNA count, number of breakpoints, the pan-cancer SCNA counts per sample) and fraction of genome altered. cBioPortal's FGA is the summed length of segments with |log2| > 0.1 divided by genome length. The CINmetrics comparison of six burden metrics (TAI, modified TAI, CNA count, breakpoints, altered base segments, FGA) across TCGA found that they do not always agree and warns against treating them as interchangeable. The wording 'number of CNAs' literally implies a count of events or segments. Since the source paper's metric is unknown, the robust approach is to compute both and report whether they agree.
